analysis.one_liner: Requires rent-to-own stores to disclose total costs and curbs their repossession and collection practices.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 53 cosponsors from both parties, but never received a committee hearing or floor vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let people with little cash take home furniture, appliances, and electronics by paying week to week. Renters who pay to the end often spend two to three times the cash price. This bill would have required stores to state, on a label and in writing, the total number and dollar amount of payments needed to own the item, restricted repossession and collection tactics, guaranteed a window to reinstate a lapsed agreement, and let consumers sue for violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households who use rent-to-own agreements and would finally see the full cost of ownership before signing, keep rights to reinstate after missing a payment, and gain the ability to sue merchants over abusive practices.

how_it_helps.text: Requires merchants to disclose, at signing and on a point-of-sale tag, the total number and dollar amount of payments needed to own the item, plus the cash price and whether the item is new or used [S3].

Guarantees customers who miss a payment a 7-day window to reinstate without losing progress toward ownership, and a 30- to 90-day window after surrendering the property, extending to 90 days for those who have paid 60% of the total [S3].
Bans contracts containing confessions of judgment, wage assignments, and waivers of the customer's legal claims, and bars security interests in goods other than the rented item itself [S3].
Restricts collection and repossession tactics, including contacting the customer's workplace, calling outside 8 a.m. to 9 p.m., harassment, and contacting third parties about the debt [S3].
Lets consumers sue in federal court for actual damages plus at least $100 for willful violations, and requires written receipts for cash and money-order payments [S3].
Sets a federal floor without overriding stronger state consumer laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own merchants, who would bear the cost of new disclosures, labels, paperwork, and exposure to customer lawsuits, and would lose revenue from customers who drop out once they see the true total cost.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall mainly on merchants, and some of that cost could be passed on to customers through higher rental payments [S3].
Disclosure alone does not lower the underlying price: a customer who sees the full cost still pays a large multiple of the cash price to own the item, and the bill does not cap total charges [S3].

The bill leaves enforcement partly to individual consumers, whose lawsuits are limited to a one-year window and can be defeated if the merchant shows it followed reasonable compliance procedures or corrected errors within 15 days [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine information gap: rent-to-own customers are typically lower-income, and the total cost of ownership was rarely clear before signing. The strongest fair criticism is that it would inform customers about high prices without restraining them, and some compliance cost might reach those same customers as higher payments. On balance the protections were modest, targeted, and similar to rules already applied to other consumer credit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Banking Committee and then to its consumer credit subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing or markup until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Larry LaRocco introduced the bill on July 29, 1993, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs [S5].
On August 3, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Credit and Insurance, where it stayed [S5].
It attracted 53 cosponsors: 30 Democrats and 23 Republicans [S4].
No further action appears in the record for the remainder of the 103rd Congress, which ended January 3, 1995; the bill never reached the House floor or the Senate [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rent-to-own merchants came out ahead: they continued operating under state-by-state rules without federal disclosure or collection-practice requirements, and customers kept bearing the full cost of agreements they could not easily see through.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rent-to-own merchants, who kept operating without federal rules

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship split across party lines from the start: 30 Democrats and 23 Republicans signed on, so the bill's death in committee was not a partisan vote.

industries.note: These stores sell ownership in weekly installments that commonly total far more than the cash price, to customers who often cannot qualify for regular credit. The bill would have forced full price disclosure, reinstatement rights, and curbs on repossession and collection, cutting into a profit model that depends on customers not seeing the full cost up front.
The bill would have required ads that quote a payment to also state the total cost of ownership, but it explicitly shielded media owners and staff from liability for ad violations.
